prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Alas! and am I born for this, To wear this slavish chain? Deprived of all created bliss, Through hardship, toil and pain! How long have I in bondage lain, And languished to be free! Alas! and must I still complain— Deprived of liberty. Oh, Heaven! and is there no relief This side the silent grave— To soothe the pain—to quell the grief And anguish of a slave? Come Liberty, thou cheerful sound, Roll through my ravished ears! Come, let my grief in joys be drowned, And drive away my fears. Say unto foul oppression, Cease: Ye tyrants rage no more, And let the joyful trump of peace, Now bid the vassal soar. Soar on the pinions of that dove Which long has cooed for thee, And breathed her notes from Afric’s grove, The sound of Liberty. Oh, Liberty! thou golden prize, So often sought by blood— We crave thy sacred sun to rise, The gift of nature’s God! Bid Slavery hide her haggard face, And barbarism fly: I scorn to see the sad disgrace In which enslaved I lie. Dear Liberty! upon thy breast, I languish to respire; And like the Swan unto her nest, I’d like to thy smiles retire. Oh, blest asylum—heavenly balm! Unto thy boughs I flee— And in thy shades the storm shall calm, With songs of Liberty!

Because the original text is a historic 19th-century poem (*"On Liberty and Slavery"* by George Moses Horton), polishing it depends on how you plan to use it. 

Below are two high-level options: 
1. **An Eloquent & Powerful Prose Adaptation** (ideal for a speech, essay, or formal statement).
2. **A Polished & Elevated Verse Version** (maintaining the original poetic structure while enhancing rhythm, vocabulary, and flow).

---

### Option 1: Eloquent & Professional Prose Adaptation

> Was I truly born for this—to bear the humiliating burden of these slavish chains? Stripped of every joy in existence, my life has been defined entirely by relentless toil, hardship, and pain. For far too long, I have languished in bondage, aching for the touch of freedom. Must I endlessly lament this total deprivation of my natural right to liberty?
> 
> I ask of Heaven: is there no solace to be found on this side of the silent grave? Is there no respite to soothe the agony, quell the despair, and ease the profound anguish of an enslaved soul? 
> 
> Come, divine Liberty—let your uplifting melody resonate within me. Drown my sorrow in your joy and banish all my fears. Command this vile oppression to cease, and declare that tyrants shall rage no longer. Let the triumphant trumpet of peace announce that the oppressed may finally soar—rising on the wings of the peaceful dove that has long cooed from the African grove, singing the timeless song of freedom.
> 
> Oh, Liberty! You are a golden and sacred prize, so often sought through sacrifice. We pray for your divine sun to rise—a natural right bestowed upon us by the Creator. Force the haggard face of slavery into hiding, and banish such barbarism forever. I refuse to accept the profound disgrace of the bondage in which I am held.
> 
> Beloved Liberty, I yearn to rest in your embrace, returning to your warmth as a swan retreats to her nest. You are a blessed sanctuary and a heavenly balm. I flee to your protective shelter, where the storms of life shall grow calm, replaced forever by songs of freedom.

---

### Option 2: Elevated & Polished Poetic Version

> Alas! Was I created but to bear  
> This wretched, slavish chain?  
> Deprived of joy, condemned to share  
> Such hardship, toil, and pain?  
> 
> How long in bondage have I lain,  
> And languished to be free!  
> Must I forever thus complain,  
> Bereft of liberty?  
> 
> O Heaven! Is there no relief  
> Prior to the silent grave,  
> To soothe the pain, to quell the grief

> Re-echo in my ears;  
> Let sorrow in thy joy be drowned,  
> And drive away my fears.  
> 
> Command oppression now to cease;  
> Bid tyrants rage no more;  
> And let the herald trump of peace  
> Bid the bound captive soar—  
> 
> Soar on the pinions of that dove  
> Which long has cooed for thee,  
> And echoed from the sacred grove  
> The song of Liberty.  
> 
> O Liberty, thou golden prize,  
> Bought so oft by blood—  
> We pray thy sacred sun may rise,  
> The gift of nature’s God!  
> 
> Bid Slavery hide her haggard face,  
> And barbarism die;

> I languish to respire;  
> And like the swan unto her nest,

> 
> O blessed refuge, heavenly balm!  
> Beneath thy boughs I flee;  
> Where every tempest grows a calm,  
> Filled with thy Liberty!

Is it truly my destiny to spend my life constrained by the heavy weight of servitude? I am stripped of every earthly happiness, forced instead to endure relentless physical labor, agony, and endless distress. For an immense length of time, I have remained trapped in captivity, constantly aching to be unburdened. Must I spend my remaining days voicing this tragedy simply because I am denied my fundamental rights?

I plead to the heavens to know if any comfort exists before I reach the quiet of death—any remedy capable of easing the overwhelming torment, sorrow, and mental anguish of a person in bondage. I call out for the uplifting concept of emancipation to echo clearly in my hearing. Let liberation submerge my suffering in a sea of joy and banish all of my terror.

May a voice command this cruel subjugation to end and order ruthless captors to cease their furious dominance. Let a victorious herald of harmony announce that the bound laborer may finally ascend. Rise upward upon the wings of that peaceful bird, whose calls for emancipation have resonated across time, originating from the dense woods of Africa.

Freedom is a precious treasure that people throughout history have given their blood to achieve. We deeply desire its sacred light to shine upon us, as it is an inherent entitlement bestowed by the Creator. May the hideous reality of forced labor be forced into hiding and all brutal cruelty be cast away, for I despise the deeply embarrassing condition of my current enslavement.

I desperately long to breathe freely while cradled by liberation. Much like a swan returning home to rest in its nest, I wish to find comfort in the reassuring presence of independence. It serves as a sacred refuge and a divine healing salve. By fleeing into its protective shelter, the tempest of my existence will grow peaceful, surrounded by triumphant melodies of freedom.

Here is a complete, well-structured text expanding upon the provided bullet points:

***

### The Cry for Liberation: A Reflection on Bondage and Sacred Freedom

Throughout the verses of the poem, the speaker delivers a poignant and powerful indictment of human bondage, articulating the profound toll exacted by a life spent in slavery. With deep grief, the speaker laments not only the relentless physical hardships—the exhausted limbs and grueling labor—but also the devastating emotional agony that corrodes the spirit. To exist in such a state is to endure an ongoing assault on human dignity, a brutal reality that strips individuals of their autonomy and leaves deep, invisible scars upon the soul. 

Amidst this darkness, the speaker’s heart reaches out toward a single, desperate desire: the promise of liberty. There is an earnest, burning longing for freedom—a force powerful enough to finally drown out the pervasive terror of the whip and the chain. The speaker envisions liberty not merely as a change in legal status, but as a transformative power capable of turning deep-seated grief into unbridled joy, replacing a lifetime of apprehension with profound serenity. 

Consequently, the poem rises to a fervent crescendo, demanding an immediate and uncompromising end to all forms of oppression and tyranny. The speaker holds up the institution of slavery to the light of justice, scorning it as a barbaric disgrace to humanity and an unspeakable blot on civilized society. Cruelty is stripped of its justifications, exposing tyranny for the hollow, immoral force that it is.

In stark contrast to the savagery of bondage, liberty is portrayed as a sacred golden prize—a treasure beyond measure. Crucially, the speaker framing freedom not as a privilege to be granted or revoked by human masters, but as a fundamental, inalienable right bestowed directly by God. Because it is divinely ordained, the denial of freedom is presented as an offense against Heaven itself, asserting that every human soul is inherently born to be free.

Ultimately, freedom is envisioned as the ultimate restorative force: a comforting sanctuary for the weary and a heavenly balm for the broken-hearted. It offers a safe haven where the tormented can finally find respite, bringing a lasting, tranquil peace to those who have suffered for so long. Through this vision of divine liberation, the poem serves as both a heartbreaking testimony to human suffering and an enduring testament to the indestructible longing for peace, justice, and self-determination.
outputs.L4:
**An Invocation to Liberty: A Lament for the Bound**

O Liberty! Thou sacred, radiant light,
Where hast thou fled across this shadowed land?
While buried in the deep, unyielding night,
Thy children bleed beneath the tyrant’s hand.
Doth not thy spirit hear the mournful cry
That rises from the soil of our despair?
Canst thou behold beneath the open sky
The bitter weight of chains we forced to bear?

Hear how the iron clanks upon the stone,
Bound to the weary wrist, the bleeding feet;
The air is heavy with a mother’s groan,
Where stolen souls and silent sorrows meet.
Torn from the arms of love, condemned to toil,
The child is bartered and the father sold—
Their sweat and tears poured out upon the soil
To swell the greed of hearts corrupt and cold.

Can Heaven look upon this monstrous shame,
Where man claims ownership of human flesh?
To brand God’s image with a master’s name,
And weave the nets of bondage strong and fresh?
Oh, hypocrites who preach of rights and grace,
Yet build your wealth upon a captive’s groans!
You paint your glory on a ruined race,
And pave your empires with a brother’s bones.

Yet deep within the bruised and battered chest,
A spark immortal mocks the whip and chain;
The spirit will not lie in quiet rest,
Nor shall the dream of freedom live in vain.
Though flesh may break beneath the heavy yoke,
And sorrow bend the knee to dark despair,
The longing that no tyrant ever broke
Still burns within, a silent, unquenched prayer.

Arise, O Liberty! Stretch forth thy hand!
Break down the walls of tyranny and greed!
Let justice thunder through this burdened land,
And set the bruised and broken captive freed!
For freedom is no gift of mortal kings,
Nor grace bestowed by laws of earthly mold—
It is the breath of Heaven on human wings,
A natural right more dear than refined gold.

Let every yoke be snapped, every chain unbound,
Let song replace the long and weeping night!
Till freedom echoes over all the ground,
And all mankind walks equal in the light.
outputs.L5:
The wind whistled softly **through** the hollow corridors of the ancient house, carrying with it the faint scent of rain and dry pine. For decades, the grand estate had been **deprived** of the laughter and warmth that once filled its rooms, left instead to decay in the quiet solitude of the valley. Dusty sheets draped over the furniture like forgotten ghosts, and the garden outside had long been swallowed by wild brambles.

I stepped carefully across the creaking floorboards, watching the amber twilight filter through the tall, arched windows. I had returned hoping to reclaim a piece of the past, to catch a lingering echo of the bright summer days of my youth. 

**Alas**, time is a thief that never returns what it steals. The grand piano in the corner sat hopelessly out of tune, its ivory keys chipped and mute. The portraits on the walls stared down with faded eyes, their stories lost to the march of years. 

Yet, as I pushed **through** the heavy glass doors leading out to the balcony, the cool evening air rushed in to meet me. Though the house had been **deprived** of its former glory, the sweeping view of the mountains remained unchanged, magnificent and eternal. **Alas**, we cannot turn back the clock to relive what has slipped away, but we can honor the beauty of what once was as we journey forward into the twilight.

counterfactuals.output:
The heavy chain doth gall my wrist,
  The lash hath scarred my frame;
Beneath the driver's cruel fist,
  I weep in silent shame.

They tore my babe from out my arms
  Ere dawn had kissed the sky;
They sold her to the distant south,
  And mocked my bitter cry.

My hands have tilled the fertile soil,
  Yet no reward I bear;
I sow the seed in weary toil,
  And reap but dark despair.

O God of Right! Dost Thou not heed
  The captive’s mournful groan?
How long shall wickedness prevail,
  And Justice weep alone?

Upon the darkling night I gaze,
  To seek the Northern Star;
Its silver beam of promise shines
  So distant and so far.

The forest bird flies unconfined,
  And sings upon the tree;
While I in heavy fetters pine,
  And dream of Liberty.

Break Thou the yoke, Almighty Lord!
  Unbind the galling chain;
Let Freedom’s holy morning dawn,
  And cleanse this land of stain.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate the text of George Moses Horton's famous poem "On Liberty and Slavery."
counterfactuals.output:
Here is the text of **"On Liberty and Slavery"** by George Moses Horton, originally published in his 1829 collection *The Hope of Liberty*:

***

**On Liberty and Slavery**

Alas! and am I born for this,
To wear this slavish chain?
Deprived of all created bliss,
Through hardship, toil and pain?

How long have I in bondage lain,
And languished to be free!
Alas! and must I still complain,
Deprived of liberty.

Oh, Heaven! and is there no relief,
Nor pity to deploy,
To soothe my woe and ease my grief,
And turn my tears to joy?

Say, Shall I live death’s vassal slave,
And yield my vital breath,
And sink into the silent grave,
To stop the mouth of death?

Go, Liberty, expand thy wing,
And fly o'er earth and sea,
And let thy cheerful paeans ring,
To set the captive free.

Oh, let the sun of freedom rise,
And dispel the clouds of night,
And beam upon my weeping eyes,
With rays of heavenly light.

Come, Liberty, thou cheerful sound,
Roll through my ravished ears,
And let my griefs in joy be drowned,
And dry my falling tears.

Bid Slavery hide her haggard face,
And shrink away with fear,
And leave the world a resting place,
For freedom to appear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a moving, multi-stanza poem from the perspective of an enslaved person appealing to Heaven and Liberty to end their suffering. Use traditional rhyming quatrains and elevated, formal language.
counterfactuals.output:
O Sovereign Lord, who rules the vaulted sky,
Look down in mercy on my bound embrace;
Hear Thou a wretched captive’s mournful cry,
And turn not back the glory of Thy face.

Beneath the burning sun and cruel rod,
My weary limbs perform the forced command;
I bear the bitter scourge, yet trust in God
To stay the tyrant’s unrelenting hand.

O Liberty, celestial angel bright,
Where hast thou fled beyond the rolling sea?
Wilt thou abandon me to endless night,
Nor set the weeping bondsman ever free?

The soaring bird ascends the morning air,
Unchecked, untamed, to range the boundless blue;
Yet man, Thine image, groans in deep despair,
And waters earth with tears instead of dew.

Doth not the righteous Judge of all mankind
Behold the grief that stains the dusty soil?
Shall cruel avarice forever bind
The suffering soul to unrequited toil?

Though flesh be bruised, and heavy irons ring,
My spirit soars above the driver’s might;
On wings of faith to Heaven’s throne I cling,
And plead for justice in Thy holy sight.

Descend, O Freedom, with thy healing wing,
Command these heavy shackles to unbind;
That every captive heart may rise and sing,
And leave the night of tyranny behind.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about a slave begging for freedom.
counterfactuals.output:
The iron cold is all I know,
It bites the flesh, it grinds the bone.
I’ve worked your fields from dawn to dusk,
And bled upon your soil alone.

My spirit bends, my limbs are weak,
Yet in my chest a heart still beats.
I do not ask for gold or crown,
Nor vengeance in these dusty streets.

Look down upon my lifted hands,
And see the man behind the scar.
I dream of paths I cannot tread,
Beneath the guiding northern star.

The rivers run without a leash,
The wild birds fly across the sea,
How can the wind be born so wild,
While I am kept in misery?

I ask to call my life my own,
To hold my children without fear,
To walk the earth with upright posture,
Unburdened by the whip and tear.

Oh master, break this heavy lock,
And let my weary soul breathe free.
Return my life into my hands,
And give me back my humanity.
